newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria constitution draft widens president power.
newsitem.headline: Algeria constitution draft widens president power.

text.p: Algeria began on Wednesday a campaign to win support for a new constitution, to be put to a referendum next month, which increases the powers of the president but limits him to two five-year terms.

All Algeria's 16 newspapers printed the 182-article draft constitution and state-run media unleashed an information campaign to rally backing of the oil and gas producing country's 13 million eligible voters for the ballot on November 28.
While stating that the Moslem faith is the religion of the Algerian state, the draft bans politicians from using Islam as a trampoline to gain power.

But the present two legal Islamist parties, Nahda and Hamas, will be given a year to change their basic platforms, apparently enabling them to take part in the next general election, promised by President Liamine Zeroual for the first half of 1997.
The Hamas leader, Mahfoud Nahnah, came second to Zeroual in last November's presidential poll, taking over a quarter of the votes. Zeroual took just over 60 percent.

"Out of consideration for the dispositions of the current constitution, political parties are not allowed to be founded on religious, linguistic, racial, sexual, corporatist and regional basis," read the draft text.

The draft adds to the huge powers already held by the president as head of state and commander in chief of the armed forces. But for the first time, future presidents will be subject to possible trial for treason or betraying the public's confidence, by a high state court envisaged in the text.
The president will continue to name, and sack, the prime minister, conduct foreign and defence policies, oversee administration work and appoint personel to senior positions.
The draft limits the president's tenure to two terms, each of five years, making it possible for Zeroual to run again for office in 2000.
The current constitution is vague over the president's term limit. Three Algerian presidents were forced out of office by disease, a military coup or heavy pressure by influential army leaders.
The draft underlines Zeroual's bid to establish a multiparty democracy built around a strong president to pull Algeria out of nearly five years of civil strife.
It gives Algerians the right for the first time since the country's independence in 1962 to found political parties, subject to the ban on Islamic and other founding principles.
The current constitution, reflecting the views of leaders in the former one-party state and their dismissal of a multiparty system, refers to parties as "political associations".
Algeria erupted into violence early in 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election which radical Islamists were poised to win. More than 50,000 people have died since.

Some Algerians blame the then "weakened" central power for allowing the now outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) to rise to dominate the country's politics in contradiction with an existing law banning religion-based groups from competing for government.
